sections.content: The content is quite interesting as we are taught to learn Math in a more rigorous way, so we can know the logic behind everything well. However, the professor essentially just takes everything on note from the previous’s professor’s notes in terms of of the content.
sections.teaching: His teaching is enough to be seen. However, I would recommend sitting at the first few rows because he likes to explain using the whiteboard directly. Although his accent is a bit vague sometimes. you can still understand him well.
sections.grading:
20% for Homework
30% for Midterms
50% for Final Exam
sections.workload: Not much workload you just need to finish several homeworks that are asked to be written in LaTeX.

sections.content: Engaging and funny. The first half of the semester can help you to understand MATH2033 ideas quicker, else you may find the pace in MATH2033 too fast to follow and have a hard time. The lectures in final week is reviewing lectures and was not teaching anything new for the final exam.
sections.teaching:
Clear accent, always ask questions(never force someone to answer so dont be afraid) to interact and engage us to think. That was a 1630-1750 class and always take a break in the middle. I only attended tutorial class for the first half of the semester and found it difficult to understand what was going on. There were only a few students attended since first week. If you are interested in Maths you can join the tutorial session to talk with the TA which is passionate on Maths. You can also prepare your questions about course materials because the TA is kind and willing to answer questions.

In the beginning of the class, he said he will release lecture recording only when exam is coming, as his own opinion is watching videos(but skipping the class) is not a useful way to learn. He did this for midterm. However, after midterm exam, the new lecture videos were released within a week after the lectures. But I dont suggest you to watch videos because of his handwriting. He wrote quite small words and it may cause inconvenience for you to check out what he has written on the board if you choose video.
sections.grading:
Very good grading.
25% HW of 5 homeworks
25% Mid-term
50% Final
No participation or any extra points.
Exams are all closed-book. The first tutorial will teach you to use LaTex. Not using LaTex to submit homework will have 20% penalty. Considering the grading is so generous, you may lost 2 subgrades if you dont use LaTex for hw.

You can check it out on USThing. Among 98/135 samples, the distribution from A+ to F are respectively 8,11,8(27.55% A-range), 14,14,15 (43.88% B-range), 18,7,2(27.55% C- range), no D and one F.
I am a weak student with nearly full HW points, but only got around 50% in exams, still get a B-, so I really recommend those who need to take MATH2033 to enroll in this course.
sections.workload:
5 homeworks in total, excluding the Homework 0 (for you to try LaTex) which is not counting into grade.
Quite time consuming if you are not familiar with the ideas. Also you may not familiar with LaTex.

sections.content:
Note that this offering in this semester has completely different content from YM and Quoc, and I doubt this will be ever repeated again, so my review might not be very helpful, just see it as a poor guy yapping.

The instructor basically made this 2-credit course a .zip of math courses, namely 1013, 1014, 2011/2023, 2033, 2111/2121 and a bit of 2343. As one can expect it's impossible to go through all these stuff at once, so every chapter is just he explaining some concepts and theorems related the topic, and turned out assignments and the exam focus more on computation instead of proving.

Given that most students taking this course are math students, I see no reason why he's teaching all these while we can learn or have already learnt those in other courses.
sections.teaching: The instructor is a postdoc who is only staying in ust for one year. Teaching skill wise, just as bad as an average mainland math professor can be. Apparently he was assigned to teach this course just two weeks before the semester began, so he appeared to be super unprepared. He typed each chapter of notes himself which often had mistakes or typos, and honestly I have no idea why he didn't just use YM or Quoc's notes and adopt their syllabus.
sections.grading:
40% Assignment
20% Essay
40% Final

It was claimed that "I will give most people A range", which I think he did according to grade distribution on USThing. He absolutely could do it since he's leaving ust anyway, he doesn't need to follow the grading regulations.

One not so interesting thing is that there was initially a 40% group project, but fortunately he changed that.
sections.workload:
8 assignments in total. Some of the assignments have some proof questions which are quite interesting, but other are just computation.

The essay was about the Banach fixed-point theorem and reinforcement learning, not too time-consuming to do, and the main point was just to let students learn LaTeX if they don't know.

sections.teaching:
Professor Ho, Quoc structures his content well and stops to answer students' questions during class. The class is at reasonable pace and you can catch up if you happen to fall behind through staying back to ask questions after the lecture or through Professor Ho, Quoc's set of course notes.

In the end, Professor Ho, Quoc finished his course content before the end of the classes, so the last three lessons were spent on extra content as seen in Chapter 5 (he explicitly said we can leave now if we want - no one did), revision and any fun questions.

Tutorial sessions by TA LIU, Wenwei (I cannot find in the instructors list) are also conducted well with constant room for students to answer and ask questions. It can go with its own pace as the content is not included in the exam, so there is never rush.
sections.grading:
Grades are not curved. Initial course notes state that A range is expected to be 85%+ before the course, and it seems to be around the same even though I don't know the exact boundaries.

All graded assignments or exams are out of 100 marks

sections.workload:
2 credits course - 1 homework every 2 weeks, HW0 ungraded

Overall not something major to worry about. Homework tests on content in class and helps you be aware of the amount of math rigor you would need. LaTeX is required for 20% of the marks, but no prior knowledge should be needed as you can learn it within the course.

Compared to other courses, there wasn't major stress due to homework, although you do need to be aware of easy to commit mistakes such as circular reasoning to score perfect marks - most people score in the 90-100 range every homework. Refer to the provided course notes to see what theorems you can actually assume and what you have to prove. Any tools required should be in there.

sections.content:
In attached files.

The finals is cumulative, i.e. covers the whole notes, except for those in chapter 5. Meanwhile the midterms will be specified by himself. This semester, he set the limit on rational numbers

As u can see in attached files, there's some intro to Discrete Math, Analysis, and Abstract Algebra. Also imo there's some strict "how to proof" stuff, for example from N to Z or smth thereof which makes me feel like this course is kinda u're treated like a baby, assuming u know nothing, and u're thought how to do this and that STRICTLY, even though u already know how to do those, and what those are

Also, I recommend to take this course even from Year 1(like me :) ), as despite the workload, the content is quite foundational, as the title states
sections.teaching:
I'm having mixed feelings about teaching bcz the classroom setup in CYT is so terrible, and at the same time Quoc writes everything so fast in the whiteboard, so u gotta sit in a strategic spot during class, where u can see the whole whiteboard.

However, I gotta say even though there are course notes updated after lectures and his fast-paced teaching, he's quite kind on questions and even encourages us to ask questions frequently, by tutorial sessions, post-lectures, or his office hours, which u can see in the syllabus(by browsing throught goggle)

He also teaches in a unique way with some stories and humor. which makes attending class feels different from just seeing his lecture notes.

pre-midterm recordings are released before midterms, and for some reason he just didn't do that for finals and just keep uploading the recordings.
sections.grading:
You might refer to other's status for the stats, which I'm not sure whether they're reliable or not. All I remember is that Quoc said during his lectures that the HWs are usually 90-ish, and midterm's mean was about "65 or 60 smth" he said.

Grade distribution:
HW: 25%
Midterm: 25%
Final: 50%

Btw, u need to use latex for the HWs, as mentioned in the syllabus. It might take time but you'll get used to it.

Mine tho:

HWs: full
Midterm: 78.5
Final: 91

Overall: 90.125
Final grade: A

Man, should've gotten A+ if my brain didn't lagged out during midterm., as well as for the fact that we're given only 1 hour. Whereas we're given 2 and a half hours for finals.

Also, tips for exams: try to understand EVERYTHING from the lecture notes and his lectures. In fact, there are some questions in the finals that are only mentioned on the beginning parts of the lecture, which is probably another reason why u should go to lectures

The overall scores in this course must've increased though, or I'd say Quoc does not use absolute grading. For instance, my senior who took this course last year got an A+ with an overall score of 90.3, while I only got an A for 90.1 .. sad :/

5 HWs, some of them are quite easy, some are quite nail-bitting

In the beginning of the course, some of u might feel like it's too easy, but the content will be kinda overwhelming once u get into those topics after midterm, especially real numbers with cauchy sequences

sections.content:
In this course we have gone through:
Logic operators
Naive set theory
Functions (set map, injectivity, surjectivity,..
Equivalence relations
Defining naturals through Peano Axioms
Defining +&• through recursion
Order relations of naturals
Similar scheme for rationals and integers
Constructing reals from Cauchy sequence of rationals
Number Theory (mod, Euclidean Algorithm, polynomial factorisation
Algebraic structures:Rings,Fields, groups

    Instead of in-depth contents of each topics , this course aims to prepare students with the basic concepts of the above topics

sections.content:
Quoc Ho will start everything with logic, then teach set --> function --> equivalence class and quotient set --> order. Then finish the part of foundation of pure mathematics.

After that, Quoc Ho will help us build a foundation of mathematical analysis. The process is the following:
peano axiom --> natural number --> integer --> rational --> Real(most technical part if you first learn it) --> complex --> field and ring. Now, you are able to take the 2043 honors mathematical analysis!

Finally, Quoc Ho will finish this course by
polynomial set --> elementary number theory --> abstract algebra(if time permit)

Overall, the content is really high quality. I really miss the time I spent fighting together alongside my friends.
sections.teaching: His teaching style is very good, he will write everything on the board. During this moment, it is beneficial to do the proof/ learning by yourself. His notes are concise and precise. So no worries if you don't understand his lecture immediately.
sections.grading:
I got 88 in his midterm and 58 in the final. So I got an A-. Let me talk about his exam each by each. For his midterm, due to the time limit, his midterm is very compact. Btw it is close book exam, you will not fail both midterm and final if you can memorize all the details in his lecture notes. Even close book has lower difficulty, try your best to understand all the details of the proof, don't memorize.

For his final, I didn't pay sufficient time to study, and didn't clarify all the concepts, so my performance was bad. Also, he put the proof of the Chinese remainder theorem in the final question in his final! Very challenging, but very fun! Difficulty is finite, but the encouragement to pure math is infinite. BTW, nobody will get 0 marks. Do you want to know why? Take his 2001!
sections.workload: very happy, nearly 2 weeks for one assignment. The really good way to catch up on his lecture, is to pay sufficient time to finish his hw, and try to use LaTeX to improve your wording. My LaTeX skill is "taught" by Quoc Ho!

sections.content:
The content is very-much self contained.
Almost all lemmas, corollaries, theorems, etc will be introduced and proven in the course.

Basically the contents of Professor Yan's MATH110 20 years ago.

The level of difficulty varies greatly among topics.
For example, 4.1 Quotient and Remainder is quite easy, but 3.6 Real Number is quite hard to understand.

This course is a required course for pure math majors, but according to Professor Fong, Tsz Ho, all the stuff taught in this course can be learnt more in-depth in other required courses, so I am not sure why he still decided to revive this course.

The knowledge taught in this course is slightly useful to those who are taking MATH1023 or MATH1024.
I think the greatest use of this course is to help you determine whether you would like to major in MATH, as it gives you a taste of the more abstract side of math.
sections.teaching:
The course instructor is Professor Yan.
The TAs are Kailong Gao and Zhongyi Shi.

There are 2 80 minutes lectures and 1 50 minutes tutorial per week.
Attendence is not taken for both lectures and tutorials.
Professor Yan also opened a WeChat group for us, but I did not join group.
Note that I attended most lectures and all tutorials.

Professor Yan is not too good of a teacher.
His voice is loud and tone is ok.
His English is good but with slight accent.
He writes on the whiteboard with a marker, and font is ok.
He is prepared before the lesson, and gives some extra examples in addition to those in lecture notes.
His teaching speed is ok.
However, even though he tried to explain stuff clearly, he failed to do so. He often overcomplicate stuff, and I had a hard time understanding the contents. It is better to learn by yourself or wait for the TA to explain it again in the tutorials.
Also note that he spend most of the lecture time after the mid term on 3.6 Real Number, but decided to not examine the topic as he think it was too difficult.
He often make mistakes and have a lot of typos in his lecture notes (even the final exam answers are wrong!).
Also, he always receive phone calls (about 2 or 3 per lecture) and pauses the lecture to pick up the phone.
The good thing about Professor Yan is that he gives us short thinking breaks regularly, so that I actually have time to understand what he is talking about.
Bonus: Professor Yan invited us to hike after the mid term.

My TA was Kailong Gao, so i cannot comment about Zhongyi Shi.

Kailong Gao is a below mean TA.
His voice is loud but tone is lazy.
His English is meh and accent is quite heavy but still audible.
He writes on the whiteboard with a marker, and font is ok.
He explains much more clearly than Professor Yan, but unfortunately, I don't think he prepares before tutorials, as his tutorials are basically same as the lectures, and he need to look at the lecture notes before starting every new sentence. He is also quite unorganized, as he taught chapter 4 and 5 in just one tutorial at an extreme pace.
His teaching speed is mostly good though.
I also thinks that he does not communicate with Professor Yan, as Professor Yan announced that 3.7 Exponential is skipped, but Kailong Gao teaches it anyways.
He did welcome questions after tutorials and was quite helpful i terms of answering questions.

In my opinion, treat the lectures as a preview, and treat the tutorials as the real lectures. Also, please learn by yourself.

Homework only consists of exercise selected from Professor Yan's lecture notes.
Homework length varies from homework to homework, some can be lengthy while some are quite short. The same goes for homework difficulty.

sections.content:
Once upon a time there were MATH110 and then MATH2721, but they went dead for a long time. FF (Prof. Fong, UG coordinator) said in his blog that he brought back this course (with a new course code) to prepare students for studying maths in the future.

Comment from others: very similar to COMP2711

TLDR:
Introduction to different aspects of pure mathematics
Tests only include easy parts of the lecture content, also questions are ambiguous that Yan Min had to explain them several times.

Giving 3 hours to finish 5 straight-forward problems (which should only take around 1 hour) open-book cannot well distinguish students' ability.
  
The course consists of 5 chapters.

~Before Mid-term~

1. Logic

Statement: sadly the truth table is not introduced (indeed very useful), just be careful with logic (e.g. not (A and B) = not A or not B)

Implication: if A then B, A => B etc. Note that this does not imply B => A. Note that this do not imply causality between A and B (despite the arrow)

Quantifier: For all, There exists. Note that they cannot be interchanged (for all a there exists b is different to there exists b for all a)

Proof: Proof by contradiction, basic proof such as sqrt(2) is irrational

Induction: strong (assume true for all n' < n), weak (assume true for n-1), double (two variables). Note you always need to prove the base case (usually n = 1).

No offence but if you start getting lost in this part you should drop this course and think again whether you are capable of studying maths. I don't mean that this chapter is trivial, but it is the easiest among mathematics

2. Set and Map

Set: Definition, Operations (union, intersection, complement, disjoint union, cartesian product) Note the operations are consistent with logics

Map: Properties of Map, Domain, Range, Image, Pre-image. Note that you can map a set to another, instead of just element to element; Surjectivity, Injectivity, Bijectivity, (Left / Right) Inverse. Note how to use these properties (e.g. prove that f(x) is injective: f(x) = f(y) => x = y). Yan Min's proof on Bijective <=> Invertible is not so accurate, better to read off maths stack exchange

Equivalence Relation: Properties, Equivalence Class, Partition, Quotient Map. TBH this part is quite confusing at first. Note that Equivalence Relation is just generalisation of equality. Two elements are equivalent if they share the same property.

~After Mid-term~

3. Number System

Natural Number: Starting from Peano's Axioms, addition and order can be defined. Their trivial properties are proven from definition and induction

Integers: Defined based on equivalence class of natural numbers.
Rational Numbers: Defined based on equivalence class of integers
Addition and Multiplication for integers and rational numbers are defined. (indeed well-defined i.e. same result with different expression of equivalence class). Later their properties are proven.

Real numbers: Transition from Algebra to Analysis. In this course, real number is constructed from Dedekind cut (infernum of a lower-bounded set of rational numbers). Yan Min said this part is too hard and did not include it in the exam. With real numbers power can be defined (power is not taught)

Complex numbers: we want to know what is sqrt(-1), we did it, at what cost? Well, the numbers can no longer be ordered. Very basic knowledge of complex numbers, such as definition, arithmetic, exponential, conjugate, argument, modulus

You should try to forget basic arithmetic you have been using since primary school. As long as it is not proven, you cannot use it. Luckily for this chapter, there is only 1 problem in final, which is related to solving linear system of equations with complex coefficients. Only DSE M0 knowledge required

5. Counting
Finite counting: Definition of counting, Inclusion-Exclusion Principle
Cardinality: comparing size of infinite sets, Cantor-Schroder-Bernstein Theorem for showing same cardinality (finding injections for both directions)
Countability: Define countability (finite or size of natural numbers), explain why real number is uncountable

The only proof-type question in final is related to counting, but it only uses simple proving by contradiction technique.

4. Number Theory
Quotient and Remainder
Decimal Expansion
Greatest Common Factor
Prime and Factorization
Congruence

Understanding techniques in finding solutions is enough. Euclidean Algorithm is very common in past papers so try to learn how to reconstruct things backward

As this is an introductory course to mathematics, I understand that the content is not in-depth

Edit at 03/2024: Indeed the course content is very useful for further study in maths, and fill in the gaps between different math courses, such as construction of real numbers, which is not taught in any analysis courses.

sections.teaching:
His English accent is easy to follow. He also knows Cantonese and Mandarin, in case you can't explain your questions in English. (Especially helpful for THAT student, if you know what I mean)

He sometimes uses weird notations to explain the content, which can be difficult to follow if you missed his explanations for them. For example, he likes to use 1-1c to represent 1-1 correspondence and a circle to represent the equivalent class of (a,b) with equal a²+b², which can be confusing. Otherwise, he explains every step detailed.

Besides, his teaching is messy. He sometimes suddenly skips from one theorem/topic to another. He also writes messily on the whiteboard, sometimes jumping from one corner of the whiteboard to another.

Lecture notes are updated nearly every week. This can be quite inconvenient for people without iPad or computer. But it's ok for me as I was using an iPad.

There is inconsistent teaching and notation between Yan Min and TA. For example, Yan Min says that the definition of the exponential operator is an optional topic, but TA still teaches it anyways.

There is no exclusion to this course, hence anyone, including year 4 MATH IRE pure math students. Essentially, you are competing with math major seniors.

The mid-term and final exams were approximately 3 hours with 5 questions. However, the time limit was not strict, Yan Min allowed you to continue writing even after 3 hours had passed.

Due to the vagueness of words in his questions (What did it mean by "smallest" equivalent class?), Yan Min explained all of them before the start, but many people still asked for clarifications in the middle of the exams.

Also, you could use your iPad during exams to refer to Yan Min's notes and your own notes. Technically you weren't allowed to use the internet, but no one checked, as Yan Min was the only invigilator. Therefore, someone might be using Math StackExchange secretly. Therefore, there is no guarantee that the exams were fair.

Besides, 3 questions will be marked in each homework, and you automatically gain marks for other questions as long as you finished. sections.content:
Description:

This course covers a number of foundational concepts and rigorous reasoning in mathematics which are essential for intermediate- and upper levels mathematics courses especially in the field of pure mathematics. The main purpose of the course is to enhance students’ conceptual and logical understanding of mathematics, and strengthen students’ ability on writing mathematical proofs. Topics include mathematical induction, set notations and logic, complex numbers, inequalities, construction of real numbers, elementary number theory, etc.

Topics:

Logic: statement, quantifier, proof, induction

Set and Map: set, union, intersection, difference, map, image, preimage, onto, one-to-one, inverse, equivalence relation

Number: natural number, integer, rational number, real number, exponential, complex number

Integer and Polynomial: division, decimal expansion, prime, factorisation, greatest common divisor, congruence, divisibility criterion

Counting: finite, infinite, cardinal, ordinal, countability
sections.teaching: I only attended a few of YM's lessons, and boy were they not worth my time.
